subject: 🌤️ The fog lifts
body_text:
96 
Plus: No Palantir pop | Wednesday, November 04, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
 Presented By Kalshi 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 04, 2026
 
 
 👋 Good morning! It's a post-midterm world. In a stunning rebuke to President Trump, Democrats have gained control of both the House and Senate.

 After stumbling a bit last night, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures are up this morning, as investors get some clarity about U.S. politics. More on that below. Crude oil prices are lower this morning, as are U.S. Treasury yields. Also today, Matt looks at the financial picture of one company that's been closely linked to politics. That's Palantir. 

 Situational awareness: CVS Health has announced plans to split the $117 billion market cap company into two: a health insurer and pharmacy benefits manager company, including Aetna and CVS Caremark, and a retail pharmacy chain with about 9,000 drugstores.

 Once more into the breach! In 1,257 words, a 4.5-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: A fog of uncertainty starts to lift
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Annelise Capossela/Axios


 
   
 
 We are waking up to a lot more clarity about the election than anyone, even Democrats with the wildest imaginations, had anticipated yesterday.

 Why it matters: For investors, less political uncertainty could mean better returns, per an intriguing analysis from equities analysts at Bloomberg Intelligence.

 Zoom in: They looked at 20 midterm cycles, back to 1946, and found that returns for the S&P 500 have been historically subdued leading into the midterms and higher once they were over.

 By the numbers: The average gain on the S&P 500 in the three months heading into an election was about 1.8% on average.

 In the three months after, it's 7.5%. (These gains don't include dividends.) The analysts didn't include S&P returns this year, but a quick glance reveals that they indeed have been slumpy. Coming into Tuesday, the index was down 0.8% since August. Yes, but: It doesn't happen every time. Three-month returns after a midterm exceeded pre-midterm returns 15 out of 20 times.

 The latest: Though U.S. stock futures were in the green early this morning, under the hood some assets were faring less well.

 Shares of Republican mega-donor Elon Musk's companies Tesla and SpaceX were both down more than 4% in pre-market trading. The other side: Billionaires do appear on track for at least one win: In California, a measure that would have enacted a 5% wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets appeared headed for defeat after facing heavy opposition from Silicon Valley.

 What to watch: The AI trade is under the lens. In a race investors were watching closely , Texas elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa governor. She has suggested a moratorium on new data centers until tougher regulations can be put in place. 

 The state accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity expected in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis. Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals intended to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns , Axios' Maria Curi reports . "Data centers in space look pretty appealing right now," Musk posted late last night. Zoom out: "We expect Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek to limit the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs, and reverse spending cuts enacted last year," Goldman Sachs economists wrote this morning. They don't expect changes to AI regulation at a national level.

 Between the lines: With a Democratic majority assured in both chambers of Congress and a Republican in the White House, we're probably in for two years of political gridlock.

 Markets typically like that, says Christopher Cain, global head of equity strategy at Bloomberg Intelligence. "The question for markets was whether such a large margin of victory would be contested by the administration or accepted," writes investor Bob Elliott this morning. "Before midnight it had been accepted, and the uncertainty of a prolonged conflict appeared to be off the table," he writes, calling the gains in the futures market a "relief rally." The bottom line: While we can't be certain what happens next in markets, we do know that we'll be seeing fewer political ads — and that is enough to brighten any mood.

2. Palantir loses its wow factor
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Palantir Technologies , the AI-driven analytics platform known for its work for the military, reported better-than-expected quarterly sales and earnings and raised its full-year sales guidance, yet still its stock slumped. 

 Why it matters: Such a lackluster response to an erstwhile favorite of retail traders underscores how investor psychology has shifted from the FOMO-fueled run-up between 2023 and 2025 to today's gnawing concerns about the durability of the AI boom. 

 The big picture: In recent years, the AI software company had been one of the top gainers in the S&P 500, which Palantir joined in September 2024. 

 Its shares rose roughly 340% in 2024 and 135% last year, riding a combination of retail enthusiasm, AI-related optimism, interest in military technology and its perceived advantages of connections to the Trump administration. (The company's co-founder, chairman and top individual shareholder is billionaire Republican megadonor Peter Thiel.) Yes, but: Palantir's roughly 2,000% increase in its stock price over the last four years vastly outpaced the company's actual fundamentals, resulting in valuation metrics that ranged from the extreme to the arguably lunatic.

 Palantir's forward price-to-earnings ratio peaked at 255 times in November 2025 and was over 100 times well into this year. A fairly valued company is traditionally considered around 15 times. The S&P 500 is currently about 18.5 times. Palantir's forward price-to-sales multiple, meanwhile, topped out at more than 90 times in November 2025. 

 For those not accustomed to these kinds of measures, that is mind-blowing. As a point of comparison, the S&P 500 currently has a forward-price-to-sales ratio of 3.1 times. Between the lines: Then a funny thing happened. Palantir really started delivering the goods, financially speaking. 

 Earnings per share jumped 64% in 2024, 83% in 2025, and they're expected to rise 122% when 2026 is done and dusted. Sales accelerated too, rising 29% in 2024 and 56% in 2025. They are expected to jump 89% this year. There's more. Margins expanded, as did backlogs. Costs stayed in check. Palantir's U.S. commercial division, focused on selling software to help companies use AI more productively, saw sales soar. Zoom in: Analysts say one blemish on Palantir's third-quarter numbers — which it released Monday after the close — was that its order backlogs were largely flat quarter over quarter. 

 That might seem a small nit to pick. But it touched a nerve for investors increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the AI trade. What they're saying: "Over the past three months, tech investors have placed greater scrutiny on the results of companies across the AI ecosystem," wrote Louie DiPalma, who covers Palantir for the brokerage firm William Blair.

 "The valuations for many AI supply chain providers have been cut in half on concerns that recent growth is unsustainable." Likewise, Brent Thill, who covers Palantir for Jefferies, noted that "the debate is increasingly about sustaining acceleration against a larger base, rather than whether underlying demand remains strong." The bottom line: None of this means that Palantir is troubled. In fact, just the opposite: The company has done so well that it has become harder and harder to wow the market, or as Thill puts it, "comps keep getting tougher." 

 But it also suggests a subtle shift among the investing public toward caring about the realities of the present, rather than seeing only limitless AI upside ahead.
